bridges.description: Support the existence of the classical-theist God as necessary unlimited being with intellect, will, and perfect goodness.
Infer a necessary ground from the existence of contingent reality.
Infer an immaterial, timeless, powerful, personal cause from a finite universe.
Infer purposive agency from life-permitting order.
Infer perfect goodness from objective moral facts, equal dignity, and intrinsic prohibitions.
Withhold the classical-theist conclusion unless its premises and comparative advantage are established.
Challenge the warrant for contingency, beginning, fine-tuning, and moral premises.
Require comparison with contrary evidence and alternative explanations.
Treat nonresistant nonbelief and gratuitous suffering as probabilistic evidence against classical theism.
Keep polytheism, deism, quasi-deism, pantheism, pandeism, and other monotheisms live as rivals.

sections.title: Burdens and inference method
sections.rationale: The parties dispute the negative burden, premise standards, deductive support, and the need for probabilistic comparison.

sections.title: Contingency and necessary being
sections.rationale: Horn's proposed ultimate ground and Lataster's uncertainty objections supply a central independent route.

sections.title: Finite origin and theories of time
sections.rationale: The causal beginning argument and the dispute over eternalist theories remain distinct from contingency.

sections.title: Fine-tuning and design
sections.rationale: Life-permitting constants generate a design inference and focused probability objections.

sections.title: Morality, suffering, and hiddenness
sections.rationale: Moral facts support Horn's perfect-goodness inference, while suffering and hiddenness are Lataster's positive contrary evidence.

sections.title: Rival God concepts
sections.rationale: The motion turns on whether the routes reach classical theism rather than generic supernaturalism or another God concept.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: The affirmative answers yes and targets an immaterial, pure, unlimited being grounding all existence.
moves.warrant: Science does not settle every question of existence, while philosophy addresses fundamental and immaterial reality.
moves.inference: Philosophical arguments can address the motion's specified classical-theist target.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This passage states Horn's answer, burden, and definition, ending when he introduces the four proposed effects that structure his case.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the most basic reality that grounds all of existence
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator hands the opening to Horn and uninterrupted first-person continuity identifies him.
moves.importanceRationale: It fixes the target and affirmative burden for every later route.

burdenContact.rationale: It states the affirmative conclusion and the God Horn undertakes to support.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: The contingent universe requires an explanation terminating in a necessary reality that cannot fail to exist.
moves.warrant: Horn invokes sufficient reason, argues the universe and its parts could have failed to exist, and says an infinite contingent regress leaves the same explanatory question.
moves.inference: The terminus is identified with pure existence or unlimited being.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span preserves the complete route from sufficient reason through contingency and rejection of a contingent regress to Horn's claimed necessary ground.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there must be a reality that is necessary
moves.attributionRationale: Horn is the uninterrupted opening speaker.
moves.importanceRationale: This is a central independent route and later supports Horn's uniqueness claim.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies the inference from contingent existence to a necessary ground.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: The universe began to exist and therefore has a cause beyond space, time, matter, and energy.
moves.warrant: Horn appeals to causal intuition, reported scientific evidence, and the alleged impossibility of successively traversing an infinite past.
moves.inference: The cause is said to be immaterial, eternal, powerful, and personal.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This complete-argument span includes the causal premise, scientific and philosophical beginning support, and all attributes Horn infers for the cause.
moves.attributionRationale: Horn remains the sole opening speaker.
moves.importanceRationale: It is a separate central causal route and anchors the later time dispute.

burdenContact.rationale: It states and supports Horn's beginning-to-cause inference.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: Life-permitting constants exhibit order better explained by design than chance or necessity.
moves.warrant: Horn reports extreme sensitivity in constants, argues chance would be extraordinarily improbable, and says necessity has not been demonstrated.
moves.inference: An agent setting early cosmic conditions is offered as the explanation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span preserves Horn's complete comparison of chance, necessity, and agency for life-permitting order.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Horn's independent design route.

burdenContact.rationale: It links observed order to purposive agency.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: Objective moral facts, equal human dignity, and intrinsic prohibitions are explained by perfect goodness.
moves.warrant: Horn defends moral realism, argues unequal cognitive capacities cannot ground equal rights, and contrasts intrinsic wrongs with outcome-only rules.
moves.inference: A perfectly good source bestowing intrinsic value grounds these moral facts.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The long span preserves the linked defense of moral facts, equal dignity, intrinsic evil, and the concluding perfect-goodness inference; each stage is needed for the complete route.
moves.attributionRationale: Horn is the uninterrupted opening speaker.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Horn's route from generic cause to perfect goodness.

burdenContact.rationale: It gives the full moral grounding inference.

moves.speaker: Raphael Lataster
moves.claim: As an agnostic non-theist, Lataster rejects a burden to prove universal divine nonexistence and instead challenges the specified classical-theist case.
moves.warrant: He distinguishes non-theism from positive denial, identifies the classical attributes at issue, and later argues that disputed deductive premises and generic supernatural conclusions require comparative support.
moves.inference: The affirmative must establish the specified God, while the negative may withhold assent by challenging premises and alternatives.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This extended span is necessary to preserve Lataster's burden definition, identification of classical theism, individual premise objections, and his concluding deductive-versus-probabilistic framework as one coherent methodological reply.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I am agnostic you can call me agnostic if you like
moves.attributionRationale: Lataster is the announced opening speaker, though captions corrupt scientific names and technical terminology within the long span.
moves.audioVerificationReason: Verify corrupted technical terms and names if exact excerpts beyond the selected quote are published.
moves.importanceRationale: It defines the negative burden and method governing all his later lines.

burdenContact.rationale: It explains why withholding the specified conclusion is Lataster's motion-level route.

responseComponents.description: Rejects Horn's proposed negative burden while accepting the same classical-theist target.

moves.speaker: Raphael Lataster
moves.claim: Neither the world's contingency nor the necessary status of God has been established.
moves.warrant: Lataster says the world might be necessary and that an unexplained assertion of divine necessity cannot secure a deductive premise.
moves.inference: The contingency route cannot reach its conclusion without further warrant.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This narrow passage contains Lataster's complete direct reply to the contingency and necessity premises before he turns to the beginning argument.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we don't actually know that the world is contingent
moves.attributionRationale: Lataster speaks continuously in his opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly contests the central modal premises.

burdenContact.rationale: It identifies the unsupported premises Lataster says block the route.

responseComponents.description: Disputes both the universe's contingency and the proposed ground's necessity.

moves.speaker: Raphael Lataster
moves.claim: A cosmic beginning from nothing is not established, and the philosophical beginning argument depends on a contested account of time.
moves.warrant: Lataster distinguishes Big Bang expansion from creation from nothing and later clarifies that eternalist theories generally, not only B theory, remain live without popularity proving them true.
moves.inference: The finite-past premise remains uncertain and cannot be treated as settled.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The opening objection is selected together with its precise claim about beginning and time; the later clarification is separately recorded in the coverage audit because the smallest opening passage supplies the direct reply.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the Big Bang doesn't actually prove that the Universe came into existence
moves.attributionRationale: Lataster's ownership is clear, but automatic captions corrupt physicist names and some technical wording.
moves.audioVerificationReason: Verify scientific names and creation-from-nothing terminology before exact publication.
moves.importanceRationale: It contests the central premise of Horn's finite-origin route.

burdenContact.rationale: It treats a beginning and the required time theory as live rather than established.

responseComponents.description: Distinguishes expansion from creation and raises eternalist alternatives.

moves.speaker: Raphael Lataster
moves.claim: Design does not win merely because chance and necessity are presented as unsupported.
moves.warrant: Lataster says the ordering of options is arbitrary, necessity has not been excluded, and changed constants might permit other forms of life.
moves.inference: Fine-tuning requires justified comparative probabilities rather than design by default.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Lataster's full opening reply to fine-tuning, from the alleged default inference through necessity and alternative-life objections.
moves.attributionRationale: Lataster is the uninterrupted opening speaker.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers Horn's design-specific route.

burdenContact.rationale: It requires a non-arbitrary comparison of chance, necessity, and design.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the elimination of chance and necessity and assumptions about possible life.

moves.speaker: Raphael Lataster
moves.claim: Objective morality and its dependence on God are unestablished, while nonresistant nonbelief and gratuitous suffering count probabilistically against classical theism.
moves.warrant: Lataster says moral facts might not exist or might be natural features, and that hiddenness and suffering are more expected on naturalism or different God concepts.
moves.inference: The evidence does not secure perfect goodness and shifts comparative probability without logically disproving every God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This long span preserves the direct moral-premise objections, the intervening method qualification, and both positive evidential routes; together they form Lataster's complete answer to Horn's perfect-goodness claim.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: it doesn't prove that God doesn't exist
moves.attributionRationale: Lataster is the sole speaker throughout his opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It combines the direct reply to Horn's moral route with Lataster's principal positive contrary evidence.

burdenContact.rationale: It presents hiddenness and suffering as probabilistic motion contact.

responseComponents.description: Challenges moral realism, divine grounding, and the fit of perfect goodness with suffering.
Tests the specified revelatory and good God against nonresistant nonbelief.

moves.speaker: Raphael Lataster
moves.claim: Even conditionally granting supernaturalism and monotheism leaves polytheism, deism, quasi-deism, alternative monotheisms, pantheism, and pandeism as live rivals.
moves.warrant: Lataster says simplicity has not been quantified, some rivals add fewer assumptions, and hiddenness or suffering may fit nonrevelatory or morally different gods better.
moves.inference: Generic supernatural evidence does not establish classical theism without deductive exclusion or probabilistic comparison of the alternatives.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The extended span is needed because Lataster constructs distinct polytheistic, alternative-monotheistic, deistic, quasi-deistic, pantheistic, and mixed rival families and gives separate prior or likelihood reasons for them.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there are infinitely many supernaturalistic Alternatives
moves.attributionRationale: Lataster's continuity is clear, but captions corrupt several technical God-concept labels.
moves.audioVerificationReason: Verify deism, quasi-deism, pantheism, and pandeism terminology before exact publication.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Lataster's main argument against moving from generic supernaturalism to classical theism.

burdenContact.rationale: It identifies and motivates the rival classes the affirmative must distinguish.

responseComponents.description: Says a necessary reality does not by itself select classical theism.
Treats a supernatural cause as compatible with multiple rivals.
Treats design evidence as compatible with other agents or God concepts.
Offers morally different or nonrevelatory rivals for comparative assessment.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: An ultimate necessary explanation cannot be limited or divided among competing deities, and uniform order points to one unlimited source.
moves.warrant: Horn says limits would require explanation, multiple ultimate beings would compromise ultimacy, pantheism identifies cause with effect, and perfect goodness excludes indifferent deism.
moves.inference: The combined contingency, order, and moral routes narrow generic supernaturalism toward classical monotheism.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Horn's complete first-rebuttal narrowing argument, preserving limitation, uniqueness, uniform order, pantheism, and deism replies as linked steps.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the cause of reality cannot be limited in any way
moves.attributionRationale: Horn is the announced rebuttal speaker and speaks continuously.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Horn's principal response to the rival-concept challenge.

burdenContact.rationale: It explains why Horn thinks the routes establish the specified God rather than generic supernaturalism.

responseComponents.description: Offers uniqueness, order, cause-effect distinction, and perfect goodness against the named rivals.

retainedMajorLines.line: Rival God concepts and classical-theist narrowing

Excluded moderator logistics before Lataster's first rebuttal.
Excluded applause and moderator instruction; no new argument inferred.
Entire audience Q&A and closing transition excluded; closing references do not import it.
Excluded courtesies, organizer remarks, promotion, and outro.

Later rebuttals, cross-examination, and closings repeat, clarify, or synthesize the selected load-bearing routes; their major qualifications are recorded below, while rhetorical characterizations, peripheral examples, and speaker-reported scholarship are omitted.

coverageAudit.qualificationPreservation: Lataster's grants are conditional and expressly withdrawn in closing; hiddenness and suffering are probabilistic rather than logical disproof; his limb example is qualified as possibly not evidence of God; eternalist theories are distinguished from B theory alone and popularity is not proof; Horn's definition-versus-existence, collection-versus-qualitative infinity, moral ontology-versus-epistemology, hiddenness reasons, and convergence claims are retained in this audit though repetitions are not separate moves.

speakerAttributionReview.handoffs: Moderator announcements and first-person continuity identify openings, rebuttals, cross-examinations, and closings; authorized auxiliary text confirms two ambiguous transitions.
speakerAttributionReview.explicitAddressees: Direct names and questions identify reply targets but are not treated as independent evidence.
speakerAttributionReview.firstPersonContinuity: Long opening and rebuttal passages preserve stable announced-speaker continuity.
mixedSpans: Cross-examination interruptions are not selected as standalone moves; their required limb and eternalist qualifications are preserved in the coverage audit.
Lataster's closing technical terms are contextually confirmed by auxiliary text without replacing canonical captions.
uncertainties: Automatic captions corrupt names, scientific references, God-concept labels, and numbers.
Lataster's closing has a limited/unlimited self-correction and corrupted de facto phrase; no adverse inference relies on it.
No direct listening is claimed; selected technical uncertainty is below high confidence with a verification reason.

One route and one direct objection.
